In this lesson, you will learn about stepper motors and stepper motor circuits.
INTRODUCTIONM
Recall, stepper motors are incremental digital motors.
Stepper motors exhibit frequency vs. speed characteristics, instead of voltage vs. speed, as in DC motors.
Stepper motors are basically a motor that positions a load to a desired location.
Read/write heads in computer disks, print wheels in printers, plotters and assembly line conveyers all use stepper motors.
Due to the many applications of stepper motors, you must be able to understand their operation and be able to recognize faulty operation.
In this lesson you will learn about STEPPER MOTOR ACTION..................
LESSON MENU
STEPPER MOTOR ACTION
The stepper motor is a true digital motor..................
DISCUSSION
Each digital pulse causes the shaft to rotate a fixed number of circular degrees.
This motion, called a "Step'' is a fixed value dependent upon manufacturing.
Common steps are 0.45, 0.9, 1.8, 3.6, 7.5, 15 and 18 degrees rotation per step (DRS).
If a continuous pulse train is applied, the shaft will rotate continuously at a rate determined by the input pulse frequency.
This is a frequency, or pulses per second (PPS), vs. speed characteristic. However, stepper motors are seldom used for continuous motion.
What type of rotating machine is a stepper motor?
An AC rotating machine can be either an AC motor or an AC generator. A stepper motor is neither.
TRY AGAIN!
A continuous rotating machine can be either a DC or AC motor. A stepper motor is neither.
TRY AGAIN!
A basic stepper motor consists of four electromagnetic stators and a permanent magnet rotor.c
The stators are labeled A, B, A, and B. Where A and B may be referred to as C and D in some texts.
The rotor, which does not use brushes or a commutator, has raised nodes that are alternately magnetized North and South.
The number of nodes on the rotor determine the degrees rotation per step or DRS.
Four nodes are illustrated for clarity purposes which produce 90 degree steps.
However, actual stepper motors have from 20 to 800 nodes to produce steps that range from 18 degrees to 0.45 degrees.
What type of rotor is used in a stepper motor?
Permanent magnet with brushes and commutator.
Electromagnet without brushes or commutator.
Permanent magnet without brushes or commutator.
Brushes and a commutator are not used in the rotor for a stepper motor.
TRY AGAIN!
Stepper motors do not use an electromagnet rotor...........
TRY AGAIN!
The operation of a stepper motor is based on the attraction/repulsion principle of magnetism, just like DC motors.
Only four nodes are shown for clarity. No matter the number of nodes, the operation is the same, only the degrees per step are different.
Assume the rotor is positioned as shown. By applying a pulse to the A stator, (magnetizing it as a North pole) no rotation takes place.
The unlike poles of the A stator and "a'' rotor node attract.
By de-energizing the A stator and energizing the B stator, the rotor will move clockwise.
The rotation continues until the "a'' node is fully attracted to the B stator.
Next, the B stator is de-energized and the A stator is energized. The rotor rotates another step.
Next, the A stator is de-energized and the B stator is energized. The rotor rotates another step.
Finally, the B stator is de-energized and the A stator is energized. The rotor rotates to the original position.
Note that the four node stepper motor takes one complete cycle of energizing the stator coils to produce one full revolution of the rotor (A, B, A, B). Press the "Activate" button to view cycles.
This is not normally the case, Stepper motors use more than four nodes and it takes more than one stator cycle to complete one revolution.
For example, a stepper motor that has 1.8 degrees per step would require 50 complete stator cycles (A, B, A, B).
1.8 degrees per step requires 200 pulses for a complete revolution (360 degrees divided by 1.8 degrees).
200 pulses per revolution requires 50 complete stator cycles (200 divided by 4 pulses per cycle).

Any other combination of energizing the stator coils causes skipped steps and may cause the rotor to lock up. Press the "Activate" button to view steps.
The sequence must be followed to produce clockwise rotation.
To produce counterclockwise rotation, the sequence is reversed.
This sequence is called "one phase energized''. Only one stator is energized at a time..
The one phase energized sequence exhibits torque up - torque down action. The rotor jerks or jogs as one stator is de-energized and the next energized.
To smooth out the jerks and jogs, a " two phase energized '' pattern is used.
The disadvantage is that with two stator coils energized at once, twice the current is drawn from the power supply.

The characteristics of stepper motors are basically the same as DC motors.
However, in stepper motors, the characteristic of RPM needs to be explained further along with two new characteristics:
Let's start off with RPM.ere...............................
In stepper motors, the RPM is based on the frequency of the applied pulses even if only one pulse is applied.
To calculate RPM, you first multiply the frequency of the pulses (pulse per second or PPS) by 60 to determine pulses per minute (PPM) since RPM is in minutes.
You can skip this step if you are calculating RPS (revolutions per second) since RPS is in seconds.
Second, you multiply PPM by the degrees of rotation per step (DRS) to determine the degrees of rotation per minute (DPM). Multiply PPS by DRS to determine degrees of rotation per second (DPS)...
Last, you divide DPM (or DPS) by 360 degrees to find RPM (or RPS).
For example, a stepper motor that is pulsed at 1000 PPS and has a 1.8 degree rotation step, produces a RPM of 300 if pulsed continuously.
If the same stepper motor is used, 1000 PPS/1.8 degrees per step, the RPS is 5.

RPM is critical because stepper motors have limits due to slew rates (SR) and error free start-stop (EFSS) rates.
Next, let's talk about the Slew Rate.......................
The Slew Rate (SR) is the maximum number of steps per second that a stepper motor can use and operate correctly.
Recall that the number of steps per second depends on the RPS applied to the stators (in which RPM can be found).nd).
If the pulses are applied too fast, the rotor of the stepper motor will not have time to fully rotate before the next pulse is applied.
By exceeding the slew rate, the motor will either skip steps or it will stall.
Typical values of SR range from 1 k to 15 k PPS and are given with the motor's specifications.
This means most 1.8 degree per step motors have a RPM range from 300 to 4500.
This means most 1.8 degree per step motors have a RPM range from 300 to 4500.
Definition
If a different degree per step motor is used, the RPM range changes.
Last, let's talk about Error Free Start-Stop rates.
Error Free Start-Stop rate (EFSS) is the maximum PPS that is applied when the motor is first started or when turned off.
The EFSS rate is normally between 100 and 1000 PPS and is always less than the Slew Rate.
For the Error Free Start rate, time is required for the rotor to begin rotation due to its inertia.
This means that the PPS applied must increase slowly toward the slew rate.
If the PPS rate is too high when starting, steps will be lost.
For the Error Free Stop Rate, time is required for the rotor to stop rotating after the pulses have been removed due to its inertia.
This means that the PPS rate applied must decrease slowly towards zero when stopping.
If the motor is running at SR and you cut the PPS to 0 immediately, the rotor will overshoot the intended stop position.
What term is used to describe the maximum PPS rate that can be applied to a stepper motor?
RPM is revolution per minute and is determined by the PPS rate applied to the stepper motor. It does not describe the maximum pulse rate.
TRY AGAIN!
EFSS rate is the Error Free Start-Stop Rate. EFSS is always lower than the maximum PPS rate applied to a stepper motor.
TRY AGAIN!
Why must the EFSS rate be used?ed..........................
The stators of a stepper motor do not rotate and is not the reason why the EFSS rate must be used..
TRY AGAIN!
The rotor's RPM is determined by the PPS rate, but is not the reason why the EFSS rate must be used.

This completes the information on Stepper Motor Action.....
1. A stepper motor is a true digital incremental motor manufactured for specific "steps'' for each input pulse.
2. Stepper motors are constructed using four electromagnet stators and a rotor that has alternating magnetic nodes.
3. By energizing the stators in sequence, the magnetic fields of the stator and rotor cause CW & CCW rotation for a predetermined number of degrees.
4. One phase energized patterns apply pulses to one stator coil at a time and use less current but exhibit jerks or jogs..
5. Two phase energized patterns energize two stator coils at a time and use more current but have less jerks or jogs.
6. The schematic symbol of the stepper motor illustrates the four stator windings.
7. RPM of stepper motors equals the PPS times 60 times DRS divided by 360.
8. The Slew Rate (SR) is the maximum PPS rate that can be applied to a stepper motor.
9. The Error Free Start-Stop Rate (EFSS) is less than SR due to the inertia of the stepper motor's rotor when starting and stopping..

The circuits required to operate the stepper motor consist of a driver and a controller.
The driver circuit has four switches that supply the energizing power to the individual stators (only one switch is shown).
A low power input signal from the controller circuit (not enough power to magnetize the stator) is applied to the base of Q1. R1 limits Q1 conduction.
When the input is positive, Q1 begins to conduct, providing a path from +V through the stator winding to ground.
The higher power current through the stator winding causes the stator to magnetize.
When the input voltage is removed, Q1 cuts off breaking the path through the stator winding. The stator de-energizes.
D1 is an LED and illuminates when the stator is magnetized. R2 limits current through D1 (D1 is not normally part of driver circuits, it's used for visual checks in this experiment).
D2 is used to eliminate inductive kick back and prevents excessive reverse current flow from damaging Q1.

D2 is used to eliminate inductive kick back and prevents excessive reverse current flow from damaging Q1. Inductive Kick Back Inductive kick back is the voltage and current generated in a coil when the energizing voltage is removed. When the voltage is removed, the magnetic field collapses cutting the wires that make up the coil. Since there is motion between the magnetic field and a conductor, a voltage/current is produced that opposes the energizing applied voltage.

DEFINITION
This circuit uses the two phase energized pattern.
U1 is a counter IC chip that counts on each clock input to Pin 15. The clock input is the PPS rate.
The counter counts up (00, 01, 10, 11) and down (00, 11, 10, 01) depending on the input level to Pin 10 to produce CW and CCW rotation of the motor.
The Q0 and Q1 outputs of U1 are applied to U3, a decoder IC chip.
The decoder chip produces one high output on the Q lines depending on the count contained in U1.
An input count of 00 causes Q0 to be high.
The high Q0 output of U3 causes a high output on OR gates U4A and U4D, the inputs to the A and B drivers.
An input count of 01 causes Q1 to be high.
An input count of 01 causes Q1 to be high..................
The high Q1 output of U3 causes a high output on OR gates U4C and U4D, the inputs to the A and B drivers.
An input count of 10 causes Q2 to be high.
The high Q2 output of U3 causes a high output on OR gates U4B and U4C, the inputs to the B and A drivers.
An input count of 11 causes Q3 to be high.
The high Q3 output of U3 causes a high output on OR gates U4A and U4B, the inputs to the A and B drivers.
This table sums up controller circuit operation for counting up. This pattern produces CW rotation..
This table sums up controller circuit operation for counting down. This pattern produces CCW rotation.
Finally, the inputs to U3 for clock and U/D consists of three switches and three inverters.
S3 controls CW or CCW rotation by applying +5 volts or a ground to U3 Pin 10. When 5 V is applied, the rotation is CW. When GND is applied, the rotation is CCW.
S2 controls the mode. RUN is continuous pulses and STEP applies a pulse each time S1 is depressed.
Inverter U2A drives an LED that illuminates for all applied pulses.
Inverter U2B, R2, R3, and C2 are configured as an oscillator. This oscillator supplies continuous pulses... oscillator that supplies continuous pulses.
The PPS of the oscillator is controlled by R3. Remember, PPS can not exceed SR and EFSS rates.

Let's look at the circuit. ll schematic of the card can be viewed by pressing Ctrl S when indicated.
The stepper motor is labeled M1 and the stator windings connect to J1.
The circuits required to operate the stepper motor consist of a driver and a controller.
The driver circuit has four switches that supply the energizing power to the individual stators (only one switch is shown).
A low power input signal from the controller circuit (not enough power to magnetize the stator) is applied to the base of Q1. R1 limits Q1 conduction.
When the input is positive, Q1 begins to conduct, providing a path from +V through the stator winding to ground.
The higher power current through the stator winding causes the stator to magnetize.
When the input voltage is removed, Q1 cuts off breaking the path through the stator winding. The stator de-energizes.
D1 is an LED and illuminates when the stator is magnetized. R2 limits current through D1 (D1 is not normally part of driver circuits, it's used for visual checks in this experiment).
D2 is used to eliminate inductive kick back and prevents excessive reverse current flow from damaging Q1.
D2 is used to eliminate inductive kick back and prevents excessive reverse current flow from damaging Q1.

Inductive Kick Back - Inductive kick back is the voltage and current generated in a coil when the energizing voltage is removed. When the voltage is removed, the magnetic field collapses cutting the wires that make up the coil. Since there is motion between the magnetic field and a conductor, a voltage/current is produced that opposes the energizing applied voltage.
DEFINITION
This circuit uses the two phase energized pattern.
U1 is a counter IC chip that counts on each clock input to Pin 15. The clock input is the PPS rate.
The counter counts up (00, 01, 10, 11) and down (00, 11, 10, 01) depending on the input level to Pin 10 to produce CW and CCW rotation of the motor.
The Q0 and Q1 outputs of U1 are applied to U3, a decoder IC chip.
The decoder chip produces one high output on the Q lines depending on the count contained in U1.
An input count of 00 causes Q0 to be high.
The high Q0 output of U3 causes a high output on OR gates U4A and U4D, the inputs to the A and B drivers.
An input count of 01 causes Q1 to be high.
An input count of 01 causes Q1 to be high..................
The high Q1 output of U3 causes a high output on OR gates U4C and U4D, the inputs to the A and B drivers.
An input count of 10 causes Q2 to be high.
The high Q2 output of U3 causes a high output on OR gates U4B and U4C, the inputs to the B and A drivers.
An input count of 11 causes Q3 to be high.
The high Q3 output of U3 causes a high output on OR gates U4A and U4B, the inputs to the A and B drivers.
This table sums up controller circuit operation for counting up. This pattern produces CW rotation.
This table sums up controller circuit operation for counting down. This pattern produces CCW rotation.
Finally, the inputs to U3 for clock and U/D consists of three switches and three inverters.
S3 controls CW or CCW rotation by applying +5 volts or a ground to U3 Pin 10. When 5 V is applied, the rotation is CW. When GND is applied, the rotation is CCW.
S2 controls the mode. RUN is continuous pulses and STEP applies a pulse each time S1 is depressed.
Inverter U2A drives an LED that illuminates for all applied pulses.
Inverter U2B, R2, R3, and C2 are configured as an oscillator. This oscillator supplies continuous pulses... oscillator that supplies continuous pulses.
The PPS of the oscillator is controlled by R3. Remember, PPS can not exceed SR and EFSS rates.
